articles.title: How to Get Rid of Ants for Good (Without Wasting Money on Sprays That Don't Work)
articles.target_keyword: how to get rid of ants
articles.seo_title: How to Get Rid of Ants for Good — Step-by-Step Guide
articles.seo_description: Spraying the ants you see actually makes infestations worse. Learn the bait-first method pros use to eliminate the whole colony — and keep ants out for good.
articles.author: Global Pest Supplies
articles.excerpt: Spraying the ants you see is the #1 mistake homeowners make — it scatters the colony and makes the problem worse. Here's the bait-first method that actually works.
articles.body:
Why the ants keep coming back

The trail of ants on your counter is a tiny fraction of the colony — often less than 1%. The queen and tens of thousands of workers are hidden in a nest you can't see. When you spray a contact killer on the visible ants, you kill foragers but never touch the colony, and many species respond by budding — splitting into multiple new colonies. That's why the ants always come back, sometimes worse.

The bait-first method pros use

Professionals win the ant war with slow-acting bait, not fast knockdown. Here's the sequence:

  1. Stop cleaning up the trails for a few days. You want foragers actively running their highway so they find your bait fast.
  2. Place gel bait directly on the trails and near entry points. A slow-acting ant gel bait lets workers carry it back and feed the queen before they die.
  3. Offer both sweet and protein bait. Ant diets shift through the season. Our gel covers both, but if ants ignore one, switch.
  4. Be patient — 1 to 2 weeks. Resist the urge to spray. Spraying the baited trail kills your delivery system.
  5. Build a barrier once the colony is gone. Apply a bifenthrin perimeter concentrate around the foundation to stop new colonies from moving in.

Carpenter ants are different

Large black ants with sawdust nearby may be carpenter ants nesting in wood. These need a void foam injected into the nest. If you see structural damage, treat quickly.

articles.title: How to Get Rid of Cockroaches: The Complete Bait-and-Dust Method
articles.target_keyword: how to get rid of cockroaches
articles.seo_title: How to Get Rid of Cockroaches — Complete DIY Method
articles.seo_description: German roaches breed fast and resist sprays. Learn the gel-bait-and-dust system exterminators use to wipe out a roach infestation and stop the next generation.
articles.author: Global Pest Supplies
articles.excerpt: A single female German roach can lead to 10,000 offspring in a year. Aerosol sprays barely dent that. Here's the bait-and-dust system that actually clears an infestation.
articles.body:
Why roaches are so hard to kill

German cockroaches — the most common indoor species — breed explosively and have developed resistance to many over-the-counter sprays. Worse, spraying repellent products around the kitchen scatters roaches deeper into wall voids where you can't reach them. Effective roach control is about bait and dust, not fogging.

Step 1: Bait the harborage

Roaches live in warm, tight, humid spaces — behind the fridge, under the sink, inside cabinet hinges, around the dishwasher motor. Place small dabs of roach gel bait in these spots, not out in the open. The bait works by secondary kill: roaches that feed return to the harborage and die, and others feed on them, spreading the active ingredient through the population.

Step 2: Dust the voids

Puff a light layer of deltamethrin dust into wall voids, behind outlet covers, and under cabinets using a hand duster. Dust stays active for months and reaches the spaces bait can't.

Step 3: Break the life cycle with an IGR

An insect growth regulator stops young roaches from maturing and reproducing. Without it, you're always fighting the next generation. Our Complete Cockroach Control Kit includes an IGR plus bait, dust, and monitors.

Step 4: Deny food and water

Fix leaks, wipe up crumbs, store food in sealed containers, and take out trash nightly. Roaches can survive on almost nothing, but removing easy resources makes your bait far more attractive.

articles.title: Rodent Control for Restaurants: A Compliance-Ready Prevention Plan
articles.seo_title: Rodent Control for Restaurants — Prevention & Compliance Guide
articles.seo_description: A single rodent sighting can fail a health inspection. Build a compliance-ready rodent program with exterior bait stations, interior traps, and exclusion.
articles.author: Global Pest Supplies
articles.excerpt: In food service, rodents aren't just gross — they're a failed inspection waiting to happen. Here's the layered program that keeps rats and mice out and your records audit-ready.
articles.body:
Why restaurants need a layered program

Rodents are drawn to the constant food, warmth, and waste of a commercial kitchen. Health inspectors look for both evidence of activity and a documented control program. A layered approach protects you on both fronts.

The exterior ring

Place tamper-resistant bait stations around the building perimeter, roughly 15–30 feet apart and near dumpsters and delivery doors. Stations must be locked and secured — loose bait will fail an inspection. Load them with weatherable bait blocks and log each check.

The interior line of defense

Never use poison bait indoors in a food establishment — use mechanical control. Deploy snap traps and glue boards along interior walls, behind equipment, and in storage areas. Rodents travel along walls, so placement against the wall (not in the open) is critical.

Exclusion: the step everyone skips

Mice fit through a gap the width of a pencil. Seal gaps around pipes, doors, and vents with steel wool and sealant. Install door sweeps. Exclusion is the only permanent fix — trapping and baiting manage the problem, but sealing entry points ends it.

Documentation

Keep a service log: station locations on a map, dates checked, activity found, and corrective actions. This is what turns a control program into a passed inspection. Our Complete Rodent Control Kit includes a placement guide you can adapt into a log. Shop rodent control →

articles.title: How to Control Mosquitoes in Your Yard (Hit Adults AND Larvae)
articles.target_keyword: how to control mosquitoes in yard
articles.seo_title: How to Get Rid of Mosquitoes in Your Yard — Complete Guide
articles.seo_description: Spraying for adult mosquitoes only solves half the problem. Learn the two-front method — barrier spray plus larvicide — that gives you a bite-free yard all season.
articles.author: Global Pest Supplies
articles.excerpt: Most people spray for adult mosquitoes and wonder why the bugs come right back. The secret is treating the standing water where they breed at the same time.
articles.body:
The two-front strategy

Mosquitoes have two vulnerable stages: biting adults resting in your foliage, and larvae developing in standing water. Treat only one and the other refills the gap within days. Win by hitting both at once.

Front 1: Barrier spray for adults

Adult mosquitoes rest during the day in cool, shaded vegetation — under leaves, along fence lines, in dense shrubs. Treat these resting areas with a lambda-cyhalothrin barrier concentrate every 3–4 weeks during mosquito season. Focus on the shaded perimeter, not open lawn.

Front 2: Larvicide for standing water

This is the step almost everyone misses. Any water that sits for more than a few days can breed hundreds of mosquitoes: birdbaths, clogged gutters, plant saucers, rain barrels, low spots. Drop a Bti larvicide dunk into water you can't drain. Bti is a naturally occurring bacterium that's safe around fish, pets, and birds.

Eliminate what you can

Walk your yard after rain and tip out or remove every container holding water. Less standing water means less larvicide needed and fewer mosquitoes overall.

Make it easy

articles.title: Termite Prevention Guide for Homeowners: Catch Them Before They Cost You
articles.seo_title: Termite Prevention Guide for Homeowners — Signs & Protection
articles.seo_description: Termites cause billions in damage that insurance won't cover. Learn the warning signs, the conditions that attract them, and how baiting systems protect your home.
articles.author: Global Pest Supplies
articles.excerpt: Termites cause an estimated $5 billion in U.S. property damage a year — and homeowners insurance almost never covers it. Prevention is far cheaper than repair.
articles.body:
Why termites are worth taking seriously

Subterranean termites work silently inside walls and framing, often for years before they're discovered. By then the repair bill can reach tens of thousands of dollars — and standard homeowners policies exclude termite damage. Prevention and early detection are everything.

Warning signs to watch for

  • Mud tubes — pencil-width dirt tunnels on foundations, walls, or crawlspace piers.
  • Swarmers — winged termites or discarded wings near windows in spring.
  • Hollow-sounding or blistered wood — tap suspect trim and listen.
  • Tight-fitting doors and windows — caused by moisture and warping from termite activity.

Remove the conditions termites love

Termites need moisture and wood-to-soil contact. Reduce risk by: directing downspouts away from the foundation, fixing leaks and grading soil to drain away from the house, keeping firewood and mulch away from the foundation, and maintaining an 18-inch gap between soil and any wood siding or framing.

Set up early detection with a baiting system

An in-ground termite baiting system installed around the perimeter does two jobs: it monitors for activity so you catch termites early, and it eliminates colonies that show up. Stations are checked quarterly. For active galleries inside wood, a fipronil foam treats the nest directly.

When to call a pro

If you find active infestation in structural members or extensive damage, get a licensed inspection. For prevention and monitoring, a baiting system is a smart, cost-effective DIY layer. Shop termite control →

articles.title: How to Get Rid of Bed Bugs Yourself: The Multi-Step System That Works
articles.target_keyword: how to get rid of bed bugs
articles.seo_title: How to Get Rid of Bed Bugs Yourself — Step-by-Step
articles.seo_description: Bed bugs survive single-product treatments and bounce back. Learn the heat, spray, dust, and encasement system pros use to actually eliminate them.
articles.author: Global Pest Supplies
articles.excerpt: Bed bugs are the hardest household pest to beat with one product. The good news: a disciplined multi-step plan works — and costs a fraction of professional heat treatment.
articles.body:
Why one product never works

Bed bugs hide in seams, cracks, and voids, lay eggs that resist many sprays, and have developed resistance to older pyrethroids. Beating them requires attacking adults, eggs, and hiding spots at the same time, then preventing reinfestation.

Step 1: Reduce the population physically

Wash and high-heat-dry all bedding and clothing. Vacuum the mattress, box spring, frame, baseboards, and carpet edges, then dispose of the bag outside immediately. Heat (above 120°F) kills bed bugs at every stage, so the dryer is your friend.

Step 2: Treat with a residual spray

Apply a dual-action residual spray to mattress seams, frame joints, baseboards, and furniture cracks. The dual active ingredients handle many resistant strains that single-ingredient sprays miss.

Step 3: Dust the voids

Puff insecticide dust into outlet boxes, bed frame voids, and behind baseboards. This catches bugs traveling through spaces you can't spray.

Step 4: Encase and monitor

Seal the mattress and box spring in bed-bug-proof encasements to trap any survivors inside and make future detection easy. Place interceptor cups under each bed leg to catch and monitor bugs trying to climb up.

Step 5: Repeat in 10–14 days

Eggs hatch on a cycle, so a second treatment two weeks later is essential to catch newly hatched nymphs. Our Bed Bug Elimination Kit includes the spray, dust, aerosol, encasements, and interceptors with a full schedule. Shop bed bug control →
